lessons.title: Lesson 1: Choosing a narrow niche
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Pick a specific user and a specific repeated job for your AI SaaS product.
This lesson builds toward: Given a field you know, you will choose one specific user and one repeated job for an AI SaaS product, written as a one-sentence idea and checked with at least one person in the niche.
Big, general AI tools already exist and are often free. Small SaaS products win by being narrow: one type of user, one repeated job, done better than a general chat assistant. "AI writing tool" is too broad. "Turns a contractor's job notes into a clean customer quote in two minutes" is narrow.
Good niches have users who do the same job often, lose time or money on it, and already pay for software. You can reach them through a trade group, a forum or a local network.
Ask AI to brainstorm niches from your own experience: "I have worked in [field]. List ten repeated writing or sorting jobs people in this field do every week." Then talk to three people in the niche before you go further.
Step by step:
- List fields you know well.
- Ask AI for repeated jobs in those fields.
- Pick one user and one job.
- Check: frequent, costly, already pays for software, easy to reach.
- Talk to three people who do that job.
Words to know:
- SaaS: software as a service: online software people pay for by subscription.
- Niche: a small, specific group of users with a shared need.
Try it now: Use AI to list ten repeated jobs in a field you know, choose one user and one job, and write a one-sentence product idea. Ask at least one person in that niche if it would help.
You can now choose a narrow, reachable niche for an AI SaaS product.

check.q: What makes a good niche for a small AI SaaS product?
options: Users who do the job often and already pay for software
A job people do once in their life
A field you know nothing about
check.why: Frequent jobs and users who already pay make a product easier to sell.

check.q: Your idea is "AI for all small businesses". What do you do?
options: Keep it broad to reach more people
Narrow it to one user and one repeated job
check.why: Small AI SaaS products win by doing one job for one user very well.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Scoping a minimum viable product
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Define the one core feature your first version must do well.
This lesson builds toward: Given your product idea, you will write a one-line core flow, a not-yet list and three never rules for the first version, with the core feature fitting on a single screen.
A minimum viable product (MVP) is the smallest version that solves the core problem well enough that someone would pay. For AI SaaS it is usually one screen: the user puts something in, the AI does the job, the user checks and copies the result.
Write your core flow in one line: "Contractor pastes job notes, picks a template, gets a quote draft, edits, downloads." Everything else (accounts, teams, integrations, dashboards) waits until people are paying.
Also decide what the AI must never do, such as invent prices, give legal advice or send anything without the user's click. These rules shape both your instruction prompt and your screen.
Step by step:
- Write the core flow in one line: input, AI job, user check, output.
- List features you will NOT build yet.
- Write three things the AI must never do.
- Sketch the one screen on paper.
Words to know:
- MVP: minimum viable product: the smallest version that solves the core problem well enough to sell.
- Core flow: the main path a user takes to get the job done.
Try it now: Write your one-line core flow, your not-yet list and three never rules, and sketch the single screen.
You can now scope an AI SaaS MVP around one core feature with clear limits.

check.q: What goes on a not-yet list?
options: Features that wait until people are paying
check.why: A not-yet list keeps the first version small.

check.q: You want to add team dashboards, chat and reports to version one. What do you do?
options: Keep one core feature and put the rest on the not-yet list
check.why: An MVP solves the core problem first.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: How AI APIs work and what they cost
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Explain how an app uses an AI model through an API and estimate the cost per user.
This lesson builds toward: Using the current price from your provider's pricing page, you will explain how your app uses an AI model through an API and estimate the AI cost per user per month, with every formula checked and the API key kept private.
An API (application programming interface) lets your app send a request to an AI model and get the answer back. Your app sends your instruction prompt plus the user's input; the model returns text (or an image, or structured data); your app shows it.
Most AI model providers charge by usage, often counted in tokens (small chunks of text, roughly parts of words), with different prices for input and output and for different models. Prices change often, so look them up on the provider's pricing page on the day you plan.
Estimate cost per user: about how many requests a user makes per month, times the average size of each request and answer, times the price. Ask AI to help set up the spreadsheet, and check the math. Keep your API key secret: never paste it into a chat, a web page or a public file.
Step by step:
- Write what your app sends: instruction prompt + user input.
- Estimate requests per user per month.
- Estimate the size of each request and answer.
- Look up current prices on the provider's pricing page.
- Calculate cost per user per month and keep your API key secret.
Words to know:
- API: a way for one program to send requests to another and get answers back.
- Token: a small chunk of text that AI providers count to measure usage and price.
- API key: a secret code that lets your app use a provider's API and is billed to you.
Try it now: Build a small spreadsheet estimating your AI cost per user per month: requests, size and the current price from your chosen provider's pricing page. Check every formula.
You can now explain how an AI SaaS app uses an API and estimate its usage cost per user.

check.q: What does an API let your app do?
options: Send requests to an AI model and get answers
check.why: The API connects your app to the AI model.

check.q: A helper asks you to paste your API key in a group chat. What do you do?
options: Keep it private and never paste it into a chat or file
Post it in a public file
check.why: Anyone with your key can use the API and spend your money.

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Prototyping the core feature
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Build a prototype of your core feature and test it with real inputs.
This lesson builds toward: Given ten anonymized real inputs, you will test your prompt, score the results and build a prototype of the core feature, improving the prompt until most results are good and showing it to at least one niche user.
Start by testing the AI job itself, before any app: put your instruction prompt and ten real (anonymized) inputs into a chat assistant and check the outputs. If the AI cannot do the job well in a chat, an app will not fix it. Tighten the prompt until 8 or 9 out of 10 results are good.
Then make the prototype at the level you can: a clickable mock-up of the screen (in a design tool such as Canva or a slide deck), a no-code app builder that can call an AI model, or a short Python notebook in Google Colab that calls an API with your key kept secret.
Show the prototype to three people in your niche and watch them use it. Note where they get stuck and where the AI output needed fixing.
Step by step:
- Collect ten real inputs and remove private details.
- Test your instruction prompt in a chat assistant.
- Improve the prompt until most outputs are good.
- Build a prototype: mock-up, no-code app or notebook.
- Watch three niche users try it and note problems.
Words to know:
- Prototype: an early, simple version used to test an idea.
- Mock-up: a picture or clickable model of a screen that shows how the app will look.
- Google Colab: a free online notebook where you can run Python code in a browser.
Try it now: Test your prompt on ten anonymized inputs and score the results. Then build the simplest prototype you can and show it to at least one person in your niche.
You can now prove an AI feature works and build a prototype people can try.

check.q: What should you test before building any app?
options: Whether the AI does the job well with your prompt
check.why: If the AI cannot do the job, the app will not help.

check.q: A test user gets stuck on your prototype's input box. What do you do?
options: Note it and make that step clearer
check.why: Where users get stuck shows what to fix.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Pricing a subscription
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Set a monthly price that covers AI usage and other costs with room for profit.
This lesson builds toward: Given value and cost per user, you will create a pricing sheet with two plans, usage limits and the profit per user, so each plan covers AI usage and other costs with room for profit.
Start from value: how much time or money does your product save a user each month? If it saves a contractor three hours, a price well below the value of those hours is easy to justify.
Then check costs: AI usage per user (from Lesson 3), hosting and tools, payment processing fees, support time, and your own time. Heavy users can cost much more than average users, so consider usage limits per plan.
Many SaaS products offer two or three plans with clear limits, and a free trial. Ask AI to suggest plan structures, but set the final numbers yourself and check them in a spreadsheet. For sales tax and business tax on software, check your state's revenue agency and irs.gov, or ask an accountant, because rules differ.
Step by step:
- Estimate the value to the user each month.
- Add costs per user: AI usage, hosting, payments, support.
- Plan for heavy users with limits.
- Design two or three plans and a trial.
- Check the math and ask an accountant about tax.
Words to know:
- Subscription: paying a regular amount, such as monthly, to keep using a product.
- Usage limit: a cap on how much a plan can use, like 100 quotes a month.
- Free trial: a short period when people can use the product without paying.
Official sources:
- IRS: Self-Employed Individuals Tax Center
Try it now: Make a pricing sheet: value per user, cost per user (including AI usage), two plans with limits, and the profit per user on each plan. Check every formula.
You can now price an AI subscription that covers usage costs and matches the value to users.

options: The value the product gives the user
The lowest price you can find
check.why: Price from value, then check it covers costs.

check.q: A few heavy users cost you more in AI usage than they pay. What do you do?
options: Set usage limits on each plan
check.why: Usage limits keep heavy users from wiping out profit.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Launching with trust and safety
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Prepare a launch checklist that keeps claims honest and users' data safe.
This lesson builds toward: Before taking payment, you will prepare a launch checklist for honest claims, data, provider terms, privacy policy and terms, and a contact route, with a lawyer review planned and a small first launch.
Trust is your biggest asset as a new SaaS. Be honest about what the AI does and its limits: say that outputs are AI-generated and should be checked. The FTC says advertising must be truthful, not misleading and backed by evidence, and it has taken action against companies over false AI claims.
Protect user data. Follow the FTC's data security principles: take stock of what you collect, scale down to what you need, lock it, dispose of what you no longer need, and plan ahead for problems. Check what your AI provider does with data sent through its API, and say so in a privacy policy.
Have a privacy policy and terms of service before you take payment; templates exist, but have a lawyer review them for your situation. Give users an easy way to reach a person, and launch small: a few users from your niche first, then grow.
Step by step:
- Write honest marketing: what it does, its limits, "check AI outputs".
- List what user data you collect and cut what you do not need.
- Check your AI provider's data terms.
- Prepare a privacy policy and terms, reviewed by a lawyer.
- Add a way to reach a person and launch to a small group first.
Words to know:
- Privacy policy: a public statement of what data you collect and how you use it.
- Terms of service: the rules users agree to when using your product.
- Launch: making your product available to users.
Official sources:
- FTC: Advertising and Marketing Basics
- FTC: Protecting Personal Information, A Guide for Business
Try it now: Final task: write your launch checklist (honest claims, data list, provider terms, privacy policy and terms for a lawyer to review, contact route, small first launch) and put together your AI SaaS starter pack with your plan, prototype and pricing sheet.
You can now plan, prototype, price and prepare an honest, safe launch of a small AI SaaS product.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Product plan The niche, user, problem or core feature is vague or missing. One page with niche, user, problem, one core feature and never rules. Includes what a niche user said about the idea. Prototype No prototype, or the prompt was not tested on real inputs. A mock-up, no-code app or notebook for the core feature, tested on ten anonymized inputs. Shown to a niche user, with changes made from what they did. AI cost estimate No cost per user, or prices not from the provider's page. AI cost per user per month from requests, size and current price, formulas checked. Shows costs for a light and a heavy user. Pricing sheet Price does not cover AI usage and other costs. Two plans with limits and profit per user on each, formulas checked. Links each plan's price to the value it gives users. Launch checklist Missing honest claims, data, privacy and terms, or a contact route. Every checklist item, lawyer review planned and a small first launch. Lists exactly what user data is collected and what the provider does with it. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

check.q: What should your marketing say about AI outputs?
options: They are AI-generated and should be checked
check.why: Honest claims tell users what the AI does and its limits.

check.q: You are ready to launch. Who do you launch to first?
options: Everyone at once with paid ads
A small group of niche users
check.why: A small first launch lets you fix problems safely.
